summary: Bulgaria is now a full Schengen member (air and sea borders from March 2024, land borders from January 2025) and adopted the euro in January 2026: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities get 90 days in any 180 across the whole Schengen Area, and everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area, have been issued within the last 10 years, and EU/EEA travellers simply need a passport or ID card valid for the stay.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Bulgaria — visas for Bulgaria

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it, but cover is strongly recommended.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Bulgaria — visas for Bulgaria

proofOfFunds.text: A commonly cited guideline is around €50 per day of stay — border officers rarely check tourists, but confirm current requirements with the Bulgarian mission if applying for a visa.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Bulgaria — visas for Bulgaria

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travellers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. There is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorisation System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travellers will need an ETIAS travel authorisation to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in — check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or the equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 litre of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air or sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.

payments.text: Bulgaria adopted the euro on 1 January 2026, replacing the lev. Cards are accepted widely in cities and resorts, but keep some cash for village restaurants, small guesthouses and rural areas — and expect some prices still displayed in both euro and old lev amounts.

safety.text: Bulgaria is a safe destination overall. Watch for pickpocketing in Sofia and at busy Black Sea resorts, taxi overcharging (use licensed or app-based taxis), and occasional rough road conditions outside main routes.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Bulgaria Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: May–September covers hiking in the Rila and Pirin mountains and the Black Sea beach season; December–March is ski season in Bansko and Borovets at some of Europe's lowest prices.

tips.text: Bulgaria is now fully in Schengen — there are no routine checks at land borders with Greece and Romania, and your days in Bulgaria count against the same 90/180 Schengen allowance as France or Germany.
Bulgarian head gestures are famously reversed: a nod traditionally means 'no' and a side-to-side shake means 'yes' — confirm verbally (da = yes, ne = no) to avoid confusion.
Taxi overcharging is the most common tourist complaint in Sofia — use app-based services or official taxi stands and check that the meter is running.
Since the January 2026 euro changeover, old lev (BGN) banknotes are no longer accepted in shops — exchange leftover leva at the Bulgarian National Bank, and double-check dual-displayed prices.
Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, apply only at the official travel-europe.europa.eu site — unofficial sites charge inflated fees for the €20 authorisation.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Bulgaria?
faq.answer: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens enter freely with a passport or ID card. Citizens of around 60 countries — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan — can visit visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen Area. Everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa from a Bulgarian mission.

faq.question: Is Bulgaria in the Schengen Area?
faq.answer: Yes — Bulgaria joined for air and sea borders in March 2024 and for land borders in January 2025. Schengen visas issued by any member state are valid for Bulgaria, and days spent in Bulgaria count against the shared 90/180 allowance.

faq.question: What currency does Bulgaria use?
faq.answer: The euro, since 1 January 2026, when it replaced the Bulgarian lev at a fixed rate of 1.95583 leva per euro. Cards are widely accepted in cities, but carry some cash for rural areas.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Bulgaria?
faq.answer: ETIAS is the EU's travel authorisation for visa-exempt visitors and is being phased in. Once mandatory, it will cost €20 (free for under-18s and over-70s) and cover Bulgaria along with the rest of the Schengen Area.

faq.question: How do I stay in Bulgaria longer than 90 days?
faq.answer: Apply for a long-stay (type D) visa at the Bulgarian mission in your country of residence, tied to a purpose such as work, study or retirement, and then convert it to a residence permit in Bulgaria. The Schengen short-stay allowance itself cannot be extended.
